entityDossier.whatItIs: The National Reconnaissance Office is the joint Department of Defense / Intelligence Community agency that designs, builds, launches and operates United States reconnaissance satellites. Management arrangements creating it and the National Reconnaissance Program were signed on 6 September 1961 by Acting DCI General Charles P. Cabell and Deputy Secretary of Defense Roswell L. Gilpatric. Its very existence was classified for thirty-one years and was declassified only on 18 September 1992.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: The NRO is the existence proof for the central premise of this board: that the United States can operate a multi-billion-dollar technical enterprise for three decades with no public existence, no line item Congress could disaggregate, and no acknowledged budget. When it was finally pried open in August 1994 it emerged that the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence did not know the NRO had built a one-million-square-foot, $310 million headquarters in Chantilly, Virginia, because the money sat in the "base" portion of the budget rather than as a new initiative. By 1996 the agency was found to be sitting on billions of dollars in forward funding that had not been reported to CIA, the Pentagon, or Congress. It is also the agency that produced David Grusch, who served as the NRO's representative to the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force from 2019 to 2021 and whose subsequent complaint alleged a concealed multi-decade recovery and reverse-engineering effort. Finally, the NRO's own 1992 declassification memorandum is a template artifact of the concealment posture: it declassified the fact of the agency and then closed with a single sentence refusing everything else.
entityDossier.narrative:
Everything about the NRO is instructive for a board that asks not whether but how. Start with the birth certificate: not a statute, not a public charter, but management arrangements agreed on 6 September 1961 between the Acting Director of Central Intelligence and the Deputy Secretary of Defense, consolidating Air Force, CIA and Navy overhead reconnaissance programs into a single compartmented office. For thirty-one years the fact of the office was itself classified. It hired, contracted, launched, and spent, and the American public and most of the Congress did not know the name.

The 18 September 1992 declassification is worth reading closely because it is a study in minimum viable disclosure. Deputy Secretary of Defense Donald Atwood announced, in Memorandum for Correspondents No. 264-M, that there is an NRO, that it is an agency of the Department of Defense, that it is funded through the National Reconnaissance Program, that its mission is spaceborne and airborne collection, and that the Director reports directly to the Secretary of Defense while the Director of Central Intelligence sets collection priorities and jointly approves the budget. It named three officials — Faga, Hill, March — and gave a Pentagon mailing address and a phone number. Then it ended: "No other information relating to the National Reconnaissance Office was declassified." That is the entire architecture of managed disclosure in one sentence. Acknowledge the container; classify the contents.

The 1994 headquarters affair is the second lesson. On 8 August 1994 members of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence held a press conference to disclose the existence of a secret $310 million headquarters complex under construction in Chantilly, Virginia, and to attack the intelligence community for not properly informing them of its size and cost. Two days later DCI James Woolsey produced a paper trail sufficient to argue there had been no deliberate concealment — but the paper trail was not the point. The point, as the Federation of American Scientists documented at the time, was that the project had been buried in the "base" part of the budget rather than broken out as a new initiative, and that base programs go essentially unscrutinized. The NRO's own headquarters project director, Roger Marsh, conceded in the agency's first open hearing: "We have been negligent, clearly negligent, for not showing the budget breakout for this project." Senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan was blunter: "This is an agency which has lied to Congress before. Egregiously." Senator John Warner put the resource asymmetry on the record — the NRO had twenty-five people working budget matters; the Senate committee had one. The NRO's own share of the intelligence budget at the time was roughly $6.5 billion.

The third lesson is the money itself. Reporting in 1995 and 1996 established that the NRO had accumulated a very large pool of unspent forward funding — figures reported in the range of $1 billion to $1.7 billion initially, and ultimately around $3.8 billion — without informing CIA, the Pentagon or Congress. NRO Director Jeffrey K. Harris departed in February 1996. The relevance to a legacy recovery program is direct and mechanical: an agency inside the classified budget can accumulate carryover at a scale that would fund an entire concealed enterprise, and the discovery of that carryover required a scandal, not oversight.

The fourth lesson is personnel. David Grusch served as the NRO's representative to the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force from 2019 to 2021, and afterward as the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency's co-lead for UAP analysis and its task-force representative into July 2022. His allegations, published by Leslie Kean and Ralph Blumenthal in The Debrief on 5 June 2023 and repeated under oath before the House Oversight Committee on 26 July 2023, did not originate with a UFO enthusiast off the street. They originated with the officer the NRO sent to the interagency table. Whatever one concludes about the substance, the provenance runs through this agency.

What the NRO has not done is speak to UAP at all. It has issued no denial, no confirmation, no historical review. It is not named in AARO's public historical reporting as a subject of interest. It has never been asked in open session what it holds. Under sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 NDAA the NRO is a "Government office" like any other and was obliged to review, identify and organize its UAP records for transmission to the National Archives by 20 October 2024; there is no public accounting of what it transmitted or withheld, and under section 1843 the postponement decision rests with its own original classification authority.

For an analyst, the NRO is best understood not as a suspect but as a calibration instrument. It tells you the maximum duration of full concealment achievable in the modern American system (thirty-one years), the mechanism (base-budget aggregation inside a compartmented program), the failure mode (a construction project too physically large to hide), the discovery mechanism (press and scandal rather than committee), and the recovery posture (declassify the container, refuse the contents). Any hypothesis about a legacy recovery program that requires less institutional capability than the NRO demonstrably possessed is, on the face of it, feasible.

claims.text: The Department of Defense announced the declassification of the existence of the National Reconnaissance Office on September 18, 1992, in Memorandum for Correspondents No. 264-M, attributed to Deputy Secretary of Defense Donald Atwood and made on the recommendation of the Director of Central Intelligence.
claims.source: https://irp.fas.org/nro/dod091802.html (DoD Memorandum for Correspondents No. 264-M, September 18, 1992)

claims.text: That 1992 memorandum ends with the sentence: "No other information relating to the National Reconnaissance Office was declassified."

The 1992 memorandum states the NRO is "organized as an agency of the Department of Defense and funded through a program known as the National Reconnaissance Program (NRP), which is the single, national program to meet U.S. Government intelligence needs through spaceborne and assigned airborne reconnaissance."

Per the same memorandum, the Director of the NRO reports directly to the Secretary of Defense; the DCI establishes collection priorities and requirements, jointly approves the NRP budget with the Secretary of Defense, and provides security policy guidance; and the Director executes NRO programs "through the Department of Defense and the Central Intelligence Agency."
As of the 1992 declassification the Director of the NRO was Martin C. Faga, the Deputy Director was Jimmie D. Hill, and the Deputy Director for Military Support was Rear Admiral Daniel P. March, USN.

The management arrangements establishing the National Reconnaissance Program and the NRO were signed on 6 September 1961 by Acting Director of Central Intelligence General Charles P. Cabell and Deputy Secretary of Defense Roswell L. Gilpatric, consolidating CIA, Air Force and Navy overhead reconnaissance under a covert compartmented office.

On August 8, 1994, members of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence publicly disclosed a previously secret $310 million, approximately one-million-square-foot NRO headquarters complex in Chantilly, Virginia, and criticized the intelligence community for failing to properly inform them of its size and cost; the committee subsequently held a hearing on the project.
claims.source: https://sgp.fas.org/bulletin/sec39.html (Secrecy & Government Bulletin No. 39, Aug-Sep 1994); see also S. Hrg. 103-997, "NRO Headquarters Project," Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, 103d Cong.

claims.text: NRO headquarters project director Roger Marsh testified in the agency's first open public hearing: "We have been negligent, clearly negligent, for not showing the budget breakout for this project."

Senator Daniel P. Moynihan said of the NRO during the 1994 headquarters controversy: "This is not the first time such a thing has happened, nor will it be, I fear, the last.... This is an agency which has lied to Congress before. Egregiously."

The headquarters project escaped congressional scrutiny because it was presented within the "base" portion of the classified budget rather than as a new initiative; Senator John Warner noted on August 10, 1994 that the NRO had 25 people working budget matters while the Senate intelligence committee had one staff person assigned to the task, and the NRO's share of the intelligence budget was then roughly $6.5 billion.
claims.source: https://sgp.fas.org/bulletin/sec39.html citing Cong. Rec., 8/10/94, p. S11142

claims.text: In the immediate aftermath the Senate passed an amendment requiring that any intelligence construction project costing $300 million or more be identified as a specific line item within the classified budget request.

Reporting in 1995-1996 established that the NRO had accumulated large unreported unspent balances — figures reported from $1 billion to $1.7 billion initially and around $3.8 billion in total forward funding — without informing CIA, the Pentagon or Congress; NRO Director Jeffrey K. Harris left the post in February 1996.

David Grusch served as the NRO's representative to the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force from 2019 to 2021, and from late 2021 to July 2022 as NGA's co-lead for UAP analysis and its task force representative, before going public on June 5, 2023.

As a "Government office" the NRO was subject to the FY2024 NDAA requirement that each agency review, identify and organize its UAP records for transmission to the National Archives by October 20, 2024; no public accounting exists of what the NRO transmitted or postponed.

entityDossier.denialPosture: The NRO has issued no public statement on UAP, no denial and no confirmation, and has never been examined on the subject in open session. Its institutional posture is the one modeled by its own 1992 declassification memorandum: acknowledge the container and refuse everything inside it.
connections: David Grusch was the NRO's representative to the UAP Task Force 2019-2021; his allegations of a concealed retrieval and reverse-engineering program originate from that detail.

Structurally joint with CIA: the DCI/DNI sets collection requirements and jointly approves the NRP budget, while the Director reports to the Secretary of Defense — a two-key arrangement that lets each principal point at the other.
The 1994 headquarters affair is the archetype for the FY2024 NDAA sec. 1687 problem: money hidden not by lying but by aggregation inside a base budget line.
Senate Select Committee on Intelligence (Moynihan, Warner, DeConcini, Kerrey, Wallop) as the oversight body that admitted it had not looked.
DCI James Woolsey and Deputy Secretary of Defense John Deutch as the officials who declassified the headquarters only under White House pressure, per FAS.
NRO is a covered 'Government office' under P.L. 118-31 secs. 1841-1843 and therefore a custodian of record within the UAP Records Collection regime administered by NARA.
openQuestions: What, if anything, the NRO transmitted to the National Archives under sections 1841-1843, and how many of its records it postponed under section 1843.
Whether the NRO holds or has held any special access program with UAP equities, and whether any such program is waived under 10 U.S.C. 119(e).
What Grusch saw or was told in his capacity as NRO representative to the UAP Task Force, as distinct from what he was later told by others.
Whether the forward-funding practice uncovered in 1995-96 was unique to the NRO or characteristic of compartmented programs generally, and whether any comparable audit has been performed since.

The identity and disposition of NRO programs historically misidentified in the UAP record — AARO has asserted misattribution of classified U.S. programs generally but has not published an NRO-specific accounting.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The DoD Special Access Program Central Office is the headquarters element that runs the Department of Defense's entire special access program enterprise. Its Director operates under the authority, direction and control of the Deputy Secretary of Defense, reports directly to the Deputy Secretary, serves as Executive Secretary of the Special Access Program Oversight Committee and Senior Review Group and Chair of the SAP Senior Working Group, and holds delegated TOP SECRET original classification authority for all DoD SAP information. It is also the Department's single point of contact for SAP matters with the Executive, Judicial and Legislative branches.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: If a legacy program exists inside the Department of Defense, DoD SAPCO is the office that knows where it sits in the architecture, who is read in, and what Congress has been told. Three provisions of the governing issuances make this office load-bearing rather than merely administrative. First, DoDD 5205.07 paragraph 3.1.g bars any DoD contractor entity, employee, representative or consultant from providing SAP material to any member of Congress or their staff without the Director's approval — a regulatory chokepoint sitting directly across the path of every contractor whistleblower. Second, the Director accredits congressional SAP facilities and "maintains records of DoD SAP information provided to Congress," which makes SAPCO both the conduit and the recordkeeper of its own conduct. Third, under DoDI 5205.11 the Director may approve the establishment and disestablishment of SAPs at tier 2 and below on his own authority with SSWG concurrence, meaning a single flag officer or SES can create and dissolve compartments. In March 2023 the then-Director, Major General David W. Abba, signed the memorandum that authorized AARO to receive sensitive U.S. Government information and effectively released NDA-bound personnel to speak to AARO — the single most consequential document in the government's handling of the whistleblower question, and it came from this office.
entityDossier.narrative:
DoD Directive 5205.07, "Special Access Program Policy," was reissued on 12 September 2024 over the signature of Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks. It cancels the July 1, 2010 version and, importantly, incorporates and cancels the Deputy Secretary of Defense Memorandum of July 11, 2023, "Implementation Guidance for DoD Special Access Program Enterprise Reform." That reform memorandum was issued three days before the Schumer-Rounds UAP Disclosure Act was unveiled and eight days before the Senate added it to the NDAA. The companion issuance, DoD Instruction 5205.11, was reissued the same day.

The Directive creates four governance bodies and one office. The SAP Oversight Committee is chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense and includes the four Under Secretaries who serve as SAP oversight authorities — Research and Engineering, Acquisition and Sustainment, Policy, and Intelligence and Security — plus the Comptroller, the Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, the DoD General Counsel, the Director of Cost Assessment and Program Evaluation, the DoD Chief Information Officer, the Under Secretaries of the Army, Navy and Air Force, the ASD for Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict, the Vice Chiefs of the Army and Air Force, the Assistant Commandant of the Marine Corps, and the Vice Chiefs of Naval and Space Operations. The Director of DoD SAPCO is its Executive Secretary. Below it sits the Senior Review Group, which the Directive pointedly says "has no designated individual as the Chair," and below that the SAP Senior Working Group, chaired by the Director of DoD SAPCO, whose voting members are the SAPCO directors of the four oversight-authority offices, the military departments, SOLIC, and the Joint Staff.

The Director's own portfolio in section 2.1 of the Directive is broader than the governance role. He is the "DoD-designated proponent" for SAP policy; the oversight authority for SAPs designated by the Deputy Secretary, "including those protecting capabilities and information shared with the DoD by foreign governments"; the cognizant authority for SAPs designated by the Deputy Secretary, for DoD components not supported by another SAPCO, for foreign-government-shared capabilities, and for "SAP studies, portfolios, and associated access management structures involving DoD SAPs"; and the DoD primary point of contact for SAP matters with all three branches of government, "including support to SAP congressional meetings, hearings, and responses to congressional inquiries." He is also Executive Secretary of the Special Technical Activities Oversight Committee established by a Deputy Secretary of Defense memorandum of 21 November 2020. He publishes and maintains security classification guides for all DoD SAP umbrellas and is delegated TOP SECRET original classification authority for all DoD SAP information for that purpose. He maintains the single authoritative repository of SAP personnel access and facility accreditation. He accredits congressional SAP facilities and maintains the records of what SAP information Congress received.

Paragraph 3.1.g of the Directive is the sentence to underline: "All personnel accessed to DoD SAPs will notify the Director, DoD SAPCO and OA SAPCO directors through their SAP CA SAPCO in a timely fashion when briefing or providing DoD SAP material to any member of Congress or their staff. No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval." A contractor employee who believes a program is being illegally concealed from Congress must, under this rule, ask the office that administers that program for permission to tell Congress about it.

DoDI 5205.11 supplies the operating mechanics. Only the Secretary or Deputy Secretary may alter the tier-1 architecture; the Director of DoD SAPCO may approve establishment and disestablishment of SAPs at tier 2 and below. New CPI enters through a "SAP project" assigned a number in the TR umbrella, and if a decision is not reached in 210 days it transfers automatically toward termination absent a waiver from the Secretary or Deputy Secretary. Access Approval Authority for non-waived SAPs may be delegated to component SAPCO staff; "AAA for waived SAPs may be delegated to the SAPCO Deputy Director or alternate designee." DoD SAPCO coordinates on personnel access requests for judicial and other federal agency personnel for waived programs — that is, the office decides which judges and which agencies get read in. The SAPOC's mandatory annual review must assess, among other things, "All waived DoD SAPs to determine the need for continued waived status."

The office intersects the UAP record at three documented points. In March 2023 Major General David W. Abba, then Director of DoD SAPCO, signed a memorandum — released to The Black Vault in FOIA case 24-F-0266 — stating that AARO was authorized to receive information relating to sensitive U.S. Government information and activities, the instrument on which AARO's repeated attempts to interview David Grusch rested. On 17 April 2024 Abba appeared alongside acting AARO director Tim Phillips in a classified UAP briefing to members of Congress. And in July 2024 former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick described briefing and testifying to members of Congress "with the SAPCO director and the CAPCO director from ODNI," saying that they had gone through everything and that none of the alleged hidden programs were what witnesses claimed.

That last item is the denial, and it is a good one to catalogue precisely because of who is standing next to whom. The office that administers waived SAPs, the office that controls contractor communication with Congress, and the office that keeps the records of what Congress was told, went to Congress to say there is nothing there.

claims.text: DoD Directive 5205.07, "Special Access Program Policy," effective September 12, 2024, was approved by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks; it reissues and cancels the July 1, 2010 directive and incorporates and cancels the Deputy Secretary of Defense Memorandum, "Implementation Guidance for DoD Special Access Program Enterprise Reform," July 11, 2023.

DoDD 5205.07 paragraph 1.2.e provides that the Director, DoD SAPCO, "under the authority, direction, and control of the Deputy Secretary of Defense, will be a general officer, flag officer, or Senior Executive Service member or equivalent appointed to oversee day-to-day management of the SAP Enterprise. The Director, DoD SAPCO reports directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense."

DoDD 5205.07 paragraph 2.1.b provides: "The Director, DoD SAPCO has jurisdiction over the protection of information contained within DoD SAPs and is delegated TOP SECRET original classification authority for all DoD SAP information for purposes of issuing SAP security classification guides."

DoDD 5205.07 paragraph 2.1.a(5) makes the Director the "DoD primary point of contact for SAP matters with agencies of the Executive Branch, the Judicial Branch, and the Legislative Branch, including support to SAP congressional meetings, hearings, and responses to congressional inquiries, unless otherwise specified by statute or regulation."

DoDD 5205.07 paragraph 2.1.e requires the Director to accredit congressional SAP facilities and to "maintain records of DoD SAP information provided to Congress" — making the same office the conduit for, and the recordkeeper of, what Congress is told.

DoDD 5205.07 paragraph 3.1.g provides: "No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant will provide SAP material to any members of Congress or their staff without Director, DoD SAPCO approval."

The SAP Oversight Committee is chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense with the Director, DoD SAPCO as Executive Secretary; its membership includes USD(R&E), USD(A&S), USD(P), USD(C)/CFO, USD(I&S), the Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the DoD General Counsel, DCAPE, the DoD CIO, the Under Secretaries of the Army, Navy and Air Force, ASD(SO/LIC), and the service vice chiefs.

DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 1.2.b provides that only the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense may alter the tier-1 SAP architecture, while "The Director, DoD Special Access Program Central Office (SAPCO) may approve establishment and disestablishment of DoD SAPs at tiers 2 and below."
DoDI 5205.11 requires the SAPOC's annual review to assess "All waived DoD SAPs to determine the need for continued waived status."

DoDI 5205.11 provides that Access Approval Authority for non-waived SAPs may be delegated to component SAPCO staff, while "AAA for waived SAPs may be delegated to the SAPCO Deputy Director or alternate designee," and that "DoD SAPCO will coordinate on PARs for judicial and other federal agency personnel for waived programs."

DoDI 5205.11 assigns DoD SAPCO the duty to notify the congressional defense committees of changes to CPI protected by DoD SAPs, and the intelligence committees for intelligence or intelligence-related CPI, and to report proposed classification changes or declassifications with a description, the reasons, and notice of any planned public announcement.

DoDI 5205.11 states that Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency oversight for administration of the National Industrial Security Program "will be phased out in July 2029 in accordance with the carve-out provision of DoD Instruction (DoDI) 5220.31" — removing an independent industrial-security inspector from the SAP contractor base.

Major General David W. Abba, U.S. Air Force, served as Director of the DoD Special Access Program Central Office; a March 2023 memorandum signed by Abba stated that AARO was authorized to receive information relating to sensitive U.S. Government information and activities, and was released under FOIA case 24-F-0266. Abba also participated with then-acting AARO director Tim Phillips in a classified UAP briefing for members of Congress on April 17, 2024.

Former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick stated in a July 17, 2024 interview that he had briefed and testified to members of Congress "with the SAPCO director and the CAPCO director from ODNI" and that all of the alleged hidden programs "have turned out to be other things that have nothing to do with extraterrestrial reverse engineering. And all of them have been reported to Congress."

DoD Instruction 5205.11 (12 September 2024) states: 'The Secretary of Defense may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as "waived" when it is determined that using standard procedures for reporting to Congress would adversely affect national security, pursuant to Section 119 of Title 10, United States Code. Waived SAPs remain subject to congressional oversight.'
claims.source: DoDI 5205.11, 'Management, Administration, and Oversight of DoD Special Access Programs,' 12 September 2024, Para. 1.2.f — https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf

claims.text: The Director, DoD SAPCO operates 'Under the authority, direction, and control of the Deputy Secretary of Defense (DepSecDef)' — not the Secretary of Defense and not the USD(I&S).

DoD SAPCO 'Functions as the DoD single point of congressional liaison concerning SAPs and verifies that the congressional offices that are approved to process and store DoD SAP information implement the security requirements in this issuance.'
The Special Access Program Oversight Committee conducts an annual review of DoD SAPs that expressly includes assessing 'All waived DoD SAPs to determine the need for continued waived status.'

The SAPOC convenes at the direction of the Deputy Secretary of Defense; the Senior Review Group convenes at the direction of the Deputy Secretary of Defense or on the recommendation of the Director, DoD SAPCO.
A new SAP umbrella may not be created until the Director, DoD SAPCO has notified the congressional defense committees in writing and 30 calendar days have passed after delivery of the notification.
claims.source: DoDI 5205.11, 12 September 2024, Para. 3.7.a.(6) — https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodi/520511p.pdf; statutory basis at 10 U.S.C. 119(f)

claims.text: Under 10 U.S.C. 119(e), when the Secretary of Defense waives a SAP reporting requirement, the information and the justification for the waiver go 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' — a channel of twelve members given the six bodies defined in subsection (g).

The requirement in 10 U.S.C. 119(a) and (b) that the Secretary of Defense submit annual reports to the defense committees on all special access programs was terminated effective 31 December 2021 by section 1061 of Public Law 114-328.
claims.source: 10 U.S.C. 119, Statutory Notes, 'Termination of Reporting Requirements' — https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title10-section119&num=0&edition=prelim

claims.text: Four Principal Staff Assistants are designated DoD SAP Oversight Authorities: USD(R&E), USD(A&S), USD(P), and USD(I&S).

USD(I&S) 'Serves as the primary interface for the Director of National Intelligence's Controlled Access Program Central Office for all relevant issues,' linking the DoD SAP architecture to the Intelligence Community CAP architecture at a single office.

DoD Component heads with cognizant authority over SAPs may 'Initiate actions to replace DCSA security cognizance activities, also known as "carve out"' and must 'Notify DCSA of activities or areas for which DCSA is relieved from inspection authority' — removing the default government industrial-security inspector from contractor facilities.

Task Force Chairwoman Anna Paulina Luna stated on 9 September 2025 that 'DoD notified Committee staff that due to the Department's special access program (SAP) rules, only members of the House Armed Services Committee (HASC) and the Defense Subcommittee of the House Appropriations Committee (HAC-D) were allowed to be "read in" on such programs,' and that non-committee Members require approval by the Chairman and Ranking Member of both HASC and HAC-D.
claims.source: House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, 'Luna Opens Hearing on Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency,' 9 September 2025 — https://oversight.house.gov/release/luna-opens-hearing-on-restoring-public-trust-through-uap-transparency

claims.text: Rep. Eric Burlison's 22 May 2026 interrogatories to MITRE demand identification of every SAP, Controlled Access Program, ACCM, Managed-Need-To-Know codeword, DOE Restricted Data/Formerly Restricted Data compartment and SIGMA category touching UAP records, and for each, 'whether the program was reported to the appropriate congressional committees.'
claims.source: Rep. Eric Burlison to Dr. Mark Peters and Mr. Christopher Land, The MITRE Corporation, 22 May 2026, Enclosure Section III.2 — https://burlison.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/burlison.house.gov/files/evo-media-document/mitre_uap-legislative-interrogatories_press.pdf

claims.text: SAP governance is layered as SSWG to SRG to SAPOC, with disagreements referred upward, and the Deputy Secretary of Defense issuing the final approval or disapproval memorandum, a copy of which the Director, DoD SAPCO distributes to the CA SAPCO and SSWG.

entityDossier.denialPosture: DoD SAPCO does not speak publicly under its own name. Its position enters the record through others: the Abba memorandum authorizing AARO to receive sensitive information, and Kirkpatrick's account of the SAPCO director appearing alongside him before Congress to say that every alleged hidden program had been checked, was something else, and had already been reported.
connections: Administers the waived unacknowledged SAP mechanism created by 10 U.S.C. 119(e); controls congressional access under DoDI 5205.11 section 7.
Reports directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense — Kathleen H. Hicks signed the 2024 reissuance and chaired the SAPOC.
Maj. Gen. David W. Abba (Director) is the signatory of the March 2023 memorandum on which AARO's authority to interview cleared witnesses, including David Grusch, rested.
Paired in Kirkpatrick's account with ODNI's CAPCO (Controlled Access Program Coordination Office) as the two offices that jointly told Congress the alleged programs do not exist.
Absorbed the Deputy Secretary of Defense Memorandum of July 11, 2023 on 'DoD Special Access Program Enterprise Reform' — issued three days before the Schumer-Rounds UAP Disclosure Act was unveiled.
Also Executive Secretary of the Special Technical Activities Oversight Committee established by the November 21, 2020 Deputy Secretary of Defense Memorandum.
Directly targeted by FY2024 NDAA sec. 1687, which conditions funding for UAP activities 'protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations' on disclosure to Congress.
Deputy Secretary of Defense — sole authority over SAPOC/SRG convening and final SAP governance decisions; the Director, DoD SAPCO reports to this office directly (DoDM 5205.07 Para. 2.4).

USD(I&S) — DoD Senior Security Official, SAP Oversight Authority, and primary interface to the DNI's Controlled Access Program Central Office; also the office to which the AARO Director reports on all administrative matters under 50 U.S.C. 3373(b)(3)(B)(i).
10 U.S.C. 119 — the statute the waiver authority runs on; its annual SAP report requirement terminated 31 December 2021.
Rep. Anna Paulina Luna and the Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets — locked out of UAP SAP material by HASC/HAC-D read-in rules per her 9 September 2025 opening statement.

Rep. Eric Burlison's 22 May 2026 MITRE interrogatories — first congressional demand to a contractor to enumerate SAP/CAP/ACCM/MNTK/SIGMA participation against UAP subject matter and state congressional reporting status.
DCSA (Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency) — the inspection authority that 'carve out' removes from SAP contractor facilities.

David Grusch — testified 26 July 2023 that a concealed multi-decade crash-retrieval and reverse-engineering effort was withheld from proper congressional oversight; the waived-SAP construct is the only lawful architecture in which that could be true.

AARO's Historical Record Report Volume 1 (8 March 2024) — asserts interviewees 'mistakenly associated' authentic classified programs with extraterrestrial activity, an argument that concedes the existence of authentic classified programs adjacent to the allegations.
openQuestions: Whether DoD SAPCO's records of 'DoD SAP information provided to Congress' have ever been examined by an independent body, and whether they would show what the twelve recipients of any waived-SAP notification actually received.
The full text and classification markings of the March 2023 Abba memorandum, and whether it authorized disclosure to AARO of waived-SAP information or only of non-waived material.
Whether any request has been made under DoDD 5205.07 para 3.1.g by a contractor employee seeking approval to take SAP material to Congress, and how such requests are adjudicated and logged.
Who succeeded Abba as Director of DoD SAPCO and what that officer has told Congress about UAP.
What the July 11, 2023 SAP Enterprise Reform memorandum actually directed, given that it has now been cancelled and absorbed into DoDD 5205.07 without separate publication.
Which judicial personnel have been granted access to waived DoD SAPs, and in connection with which litigation.
How many waived SAPs currently exist, and what is the aggregate dollar value? No unclassified figure is published, and the annual report that would have supplied one terminated 31 December 2021.
Which office maintains the master list of waived SAPs reviewed annually by the SAPOC, and does that list carry program nicknames releasable to Congress under DoDI 5205.11?
How many DoD contractor facilities currently operate under 'carve out' with DCSA relieved of inspection authority, and which Components initiated them?
Has any DoD SAPCO Director ever certified to the defense committees that no UAP- or recovered-materials-related SAP exists? No such certification is in the public record.

entityDossier.whatItIs: S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226 was the Schumer-Rounds "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act of 2023," submitted in July 2023 and folded into the Senate-passed FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act on July 27, 2023 as Division G, sections 9001 through 9015. Modeled on the President John F. Kennedy Assassination Records Collection Act of 1992, it would have created a nine-member, Senate-confirmed UAP Records Review Board with subpoena-adjacent powers, a government-wide records collection at the National Archives, a controlled disclosure process, and a mandate that the federal government exercise eminent domain over recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence held by private parties.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: This is the only time the United States Senate has passed statutory text asserting, as a matter of legislative fact, that private entities may be holding recovered non-human technology and biological material and that the government should take it. The bill defines "legacy program," "non-human intelligence," "technologies of unknown origin" and "controlling authority" in statutory language, and its Review Board qualification clause bars anyone with "any previous or current involvement with any legacy program or controlling authority relating to the collection, exploitation, or reverse engineering of technologies of unknown origin" — a conflict-of-interest screen that presupposes the existence of the thing being screened against. Senators Schumer, Rounds, Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich, several of them sitting members of the Intelligence and Armed Services Committees, wrote that clause. The Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security then submitted a thirty-three page line-by-line rewrite to conferees in November 2023 stating that the Department "strongly urges consideration" of its revisions, and the Department's core objectives prevailed. The gap between what the Senate passed and what the President signed is the single cleanest measurement of institutional resistance available on this board.
entityDossier.narrative:
The UAP Disclosure Act was unveiled on 14 July 2023 with Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer as prime sponsor and Senator Mike Rounds as lead co-sponsor, with Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich joining. It was added to the FY2024 NDAA in an agreed bloc of amendments without floor debate or a separate vote, and the Senate passed the NDAA including it on 27 July 2023.

The findings section is short and remarkably direct. Congress would have declared that all federal records concerning UAP "should carry a presumption of immediate disclosure"; that "Legislation is necessary to create an enforceable, independent, and accountable process for the public disclosure of such records"; and that "Legislation is necessary because credible evidence and testimony indicates that Federal Government unidentified anomalous phenomena records exist that have not been declassified or subject to mandatory declassification review as set forth in Executive Order 13526."

The definitions are where the bill does its most consequential work, because definitions survive in the mind even when the operative provisions die. "Legacy program" is defined as "all Federal, State, and local government, commercial industry, academic, and private sector endeavors to collect, exploit, or reverse engineer technologies of unknown origin or examine biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence that pre-dates the date of the enactment of this Act." "Non-human intelligence" is "any sentient intelligent non-human lifeform regardless of nature or ultimate origin that may be presumed responsible for unidentified anomalous phenomena or of which the Federal Government has become aware." "Technologies of unknown origin" is a lawyer's inventory: "any materials or meta-materials, ejecta, crash debris, mechanisms, machinery, equipment, assemblies or sub-assemblies, engineering models or processes, damaged or intact aerospace vehicles, and damaged or intact ocean-surface and undersea craft associated with unidentified anomalous phenomena or incorporating science and technology that lacks prosaic attribution or known means of human manufacture." And "controlling authority" reaches "any Federal, State, or local government department, office, agency, committee, commission, commercial company, academic institution, or private sector entity in physical possession of technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence." Whoever drafted that list was not speculating about the abstract; they were describing categories of custody.

The Review Board would have been nine citizens appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate, nominated within ninety days after considering persons recommended by the four congressional leaders, the Secretary of Defense, the National Academy of Sciences, the American Historical Association, and — a genuinely unusual inclusion in a statute — "the UAP Disclosure Foundation." Nominees had to include at least one current or former national security official, one current or former foreign service official, one scientist or engineer, one economist, one professional historian and one sociologist. They would have been "granted the necessary security clearances and accesses, including any and all relevant Presidential, departmental, and agency special access programs, in an accelerated manner." Confirmation ran through Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs on compressed clocks: hearings within thirty days, committee vote within fourteen, floor vote within fourteen.

The eminent domain provision, section 9010(a), read: "The Federal Government shall exercise eminent domain over any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities in the interests of the public good." Subsection (b) required that any such material "should it exist, shall be made available to the Review Board for personal examination and subsequent disclosure determination." Subsection (c) tasked the Board with deciding "whether the material examined constitutes technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence beyond a reasonable doubt." Subsection (d) gave the Board access to all testimony from UAP witnesses, close observers, "and legacy program personnel and whistleblowers" in the government's possession, and subsection (e) directed it to solicit more, extending the whistleblower protections of section 1673(b) of the FY2023 NDAA, 50 U.S.C. 3373b(b).

Other operative provisions: government offices had 300 days to review, identify and organize their UAP records; the Board was to be treated as an agency of the United States for purposes of 18 U.S.C. 6001, the witness immunity statute; the Board would report to congressional leadership, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, and House Oversight; and $20,000,000 was authorized for fiscal year 2024, with the President permitted to use available discretionary sums in the interim.

Then the Pentagon wrote back. In November 2023, during end-stage conference negotiations, the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security transmitted to congressional negotiators a thirty-three page line-by-line rewrite of the Senate-passed text, presented as the Department's "informal views" but stating that the Department "strongly urges consideration" of the changes and that the position was arrived at "after conferring with NARA/ISOO." The document was first published by Douglas Dean Johnson in July 2024. Its treatment of section 9010 is the tell: OUSD(I&S) proposed replacing the mandatory "The Federal Government shall exercise eminent domain over" with "It is the sense of Congress that the Federal Government should exercise eminent domain appropriately over" — while leaving the object of the sentence, "any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities," untouched. Asked why, former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick replied that "a compromise was proposed to allow for the exercising of eminent domain under AARO's authority to underscore that AARO could compel disclosure of anything, should anything exist. Since we know nothing exists, we didn't feel it made our job harder."

Kirkpatrick was blunter elsewhere. On 17 July 2024 he told interviewer Marik von Rennenkampff, "We convinced Congress last year not to go down that road." The Review Board, its staff, the eminent domain authority and the controlled disclosure process were all deleted in conference. Schumer, on the Senate floor on 13 December 2023, called it "really an outrage."

claims.text: S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226 was submitted by Senator Schumer for himself, Senator Rounds, Senator Rubio, Senator Gillibrand, Senator Young and Senator Heinrich, and is titled the "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act of 2023."

The bill's findings state that all federal UAP records "should carry a presumption of immediate disclosure"; that "Legislation is necessary to create an enforceable, independent, and accountable process for the public disclosure of such records"; and that "Legislation is necessary because credible evidence and testimony indicates that Federal Government unidentified anomalous phenomena records exist that have not been declassified or subject to mandatory declassification review as set forth in Executive Order 13526."

The bill defines "legacy program" as "all Federal, State, and local government, commercial industry, academic, and private sector endeavors to collect, exploit, or reverse engineer technologies of unknown origin or examine biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence that pre-dates the date of the enactment of this Act."

The bill defines "non-human intelligence" as "any sentient intelligent non-human lifeform regardless of nature or ultimate origin that may be presumed responsible for unidentified anomalous phenomena or of which the Federal Government has become aware."

The bill defines "technologies of unknown origin" as "any materials or meta-materials, ejecta, crash debris, mechanisms, machinery, equipment, assemblies or sub-assemblies, engineering models or processes, damaged or intact aerospace vehicles, and damaged or intact ocean-surface and undersea craft associated with unidentified anomalous phenomena or incorporating science and technology that lacks prosaic attribution or known means of human manufacture."

The bill defines "controlling authority" to include "any Federal, State, or local government department, office, agency, committee, commission, commercial company, academic institution, or private sector entity in physical possession of technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence."

The Review Board would have consisted of 9 U.S. citizens appointed by the President by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, without regard to political affiliation, nominated not later than 90 days after enactment, and all nominees "shall be granted the necessary security clearances and accesses, including any and all relevant Presidential, departmental, and agency special access programs, in an accelerated manner subject to the standard procedures for granting such clearances."

Review Board nominees "shall be impartial citizens, none of whom shall have had any previous or current involvement with any legacy program or controlling authority relating to the collection, exploitation, or reverse engineering of technologies of unknown origin or the examination of biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence."

The President would have made nominations after considering persons recommended by the four congressional leaders, the Secretary of Defense, the National Academy of Sciences, "the UAP Disclosure Foundation," and the American Historical Association; the Board had to include at least one current or former national security official, one current or former foreign service official, one scientist or engineer, one economist, one professional historian, and one sociologist.

Section __10(a) provided: "The Federal Government shall exercise eminent domain over any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities in the interests of the public good."

Section __10(c)(1) tasked the Review Board with deciding "whether the material examined constitutes technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence beyond a reasonable doubt," and __10(d) gave the Board access to all testimony from UAP witnesses, close observers, "and legacy program personnel and whistleblowers" in the government's possession.

Government offices had 300 days after enactment to review, identify and organize each UAP record for disclosure to the public, review by the Review Board, and transmission to the Archivist; the Review Board was to be treated as an agency of the United States for purposes of 18 U.S.C. 6001 witness immunity; and $20,000,000 was authorized for fiscal year 2024.

In November 2023 the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security transmitted to congressional negotiators a 33-page line-by-line rewrite of the Senate-passed UAPDA, presented as the Department's "informal views" while stating the Department "strongly urges consideration" and that the position was reached "after conferring with NARA/ISOO"; the rewrite proposed replacing the mandatory eminent domain language with "It is the sense of Congress that the Federal Government should exercise eminent domain appropriately over..." while retaining the object of the provision.

Former AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick said in a July 17, 2024 interview, regarding the 2023 UAPDA: "We convinced Congress last year not to go down that road," and by email on July 23, 2024 explained the retained eminent domain language: "a compromise was proposed to allow for the exercising of eminent domain under AARO's authority to underscore that AARO could compel disclosure of anything, should anything exist. Since we know nothing exists, we didn't feel it made our job harder."

entityDossier.denialPosture: The Department of Defense never denied the bill's premises in public. It filed a redline. The 'informal views' rewrite objected to structure, duplication with AARO's existing historical-report mandate, and burden on industry — Kirkpatrick's stated reasoning was that the Review Board would duplicate AARO and that 'we found no evidence of any of these allegations. None.' The Department nonetheless declined to strike the eminent domain object, which is the more interesting fact.
connections: Sponsors Schumer, Rounds, Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich — Rounds sits on both Senate Armed Services and Senate Intelligence; Rubio was SSCI vice chairman.
Modeled on the President John F. Kennedy Assassination Records Collection Act of 1992 and its Assassination Records Review Board.

OUSD(I&S) under Ronald Moultrie (who resigned effective February 29, 2024) was the office that transmitted the rewrite; AARO was administratively attached to OUSD(I&S) while its director reported to the Deputy Secretary of Defense on operational and security matters.
Sean Kirkpatrick, AARO director from mid-2022 to December 1, 2023, is the named actor claiming credit for defeating the bill.
The surviving remnant is P.L. 118-31 secs. 1841-1843; the deleted provisions are catalogued in the Joint Explanatory Statement to H. Rept. 118-301 at page 1330.

The 'controlling authority' definition reaching commercial companies and academic institutions is the statutory hook that would have touched defense contractors directly — the point at which the bill stopped being about records and started being about property.

Refiled substantially intact as S.Amdt. 2610 to S. 4638 (FY2025 NDAA) on July 11, 2024, this time with Rounds as lead sponsor and Schumer as co-sponsor, printed at Cong. Rec. S4943-S4950; Gillibrand joined July 23 and Heinrich August 1, 2024.
openQuestions: Whether the text as filed in S.Amdt. 797 differs in any material respect from the text released by the Majority Leader's office in July 2023; congress.gov is the authoritative version and section numbering in the released draft is left blank.

Whether NARA and ISOO, whom OUSD(I&S) said it consulted, supported the rewrite or merely commented on records-management feasibility.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, H.R. 2670, became Public Law 118-31 on December 22, 2023. It contains four UAP-related provisions: section 1687 (funding cutoff for unreported UAP special access programs), sections 1841-1843 (the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection at the National Archives), section 7341 (a reporting-channel adjustment) and section 7343 (the parallel Intelligence Authorization funding cutoff). It is what survived of the Schumer-Rounds UAP Disclosure Act after House-Senate conference.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: The enacted law is simultaneously the strongest and the weakest document on this board. Strongest, because the Joint Explanatory Statement of the House-Senate conference committee states in the official legislative history that the section 1687 funding prohibition "could cover" activities including "Analyzing such craft, or pieces or components thereof," "Actions relating to reverse engineering or replicating unidentified anomalous phenomena technology or performance," propulsion "based on or derived from or inspired by inspection, analysis, or reverse engineering of recovered unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or materials," and "Any aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, and electric ion thrust." Conferees do not write six itemized categories of a thing that does not exist. Weakest, because everything with teeth was removed: the same JES records that "The agreement does not include the provisions that would establish an independent Review Board, a Review Board staff, eminent domain authority, or a controlled disclosure process," and section 1843 hands the postponement decision back to "the original classification authority" — the same officials the Senate bill was designed to review. The difference between the Senate text and the enacted text is the measurable output of the concealment effort in a single legislative cycle.
entityDossier.narrative:
The FY2024 NDAA is a 973-page enrolled bill authorizing $886 billion. The Senate approved the conference version 87-13 on 13 December 2023, the House 310-118 the next day, and the President signed it on 22 December.

Section 1687, "Limitation on Use of Funds for Certain Unreported Programs," is the money clause. Subsection (a): "None of the funds authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act may be obligated or expended in support of any activities involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations unless the Secretary of Defense has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024." Subsection (b) closes the contractor channel: citing DoD Instruction 3204.01, it provides that independent research and development funding relating to UAP "shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership." The missing preposition is in the enacted text. Subsection (c) defines the appropriate committees as the congressional defense committees plus HPSCI and SSCI, and congressional leadership as the four leaders.

That IR&D subsection is the sleeper. It is a legislative acknowledgment that UAP-related work might sit inside contractor overhead accounts rather than a government program element — funded by the government as an allowable indirect cost without ever appearing as a DoD program. Congress does not write a prohibition against a billing practice nobody uses.

The Joint Explanatory Statement explains what the conferees did to the Senate provision (formerly section 1646): they removed the direction to provide information to AARO, and summarized the prohibition. Then they wrote six numbered categories of activity the prohibition "could cover": recruiting, employing, equipping and providing security for government or contractor personnel with a mission of "capturing, recovering, and securing unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or pieces and components of such craft"; analyzing such craft or components "including for the purpose of determining properties, material composition, method of manufacture, origin, characteristics, usage and application, performance, operational modalities, or reverse engineering of such craft or component technology"; protecting UAP activities and information "from disclosure or compromise"; actions relating to reverse engineering or replicating UAP technology or performance; development of propulsion technology or aerospace craft "based on or derived from or inspired by" reverse engineering of recovered UAP craft or materials; and "Any aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, and electric ion thrust." That sixth category is a definition by exclusion of every propulsion method the conferees could not name.

Section 7343 does the same on the Intelligence Authorization side, substituting the DNI for the Secretary of Defense and adding the Appropriations Committees. Its IR&D subsection contains a dangling cross-reference — "contracts covered by such instruction," with no instruction identified anywhere in the section. The intelligence committee chairmen entered an Explanatory Statement in the Congressional Record on 14 December 2023 saying section 7343 was intended "to avoid technology and security stovepipes and expand awareness regarding any historical exotic technology antecedents previously provided by the Federal Government for research and development purposes if they are shown to exist."

Sections 1841-1843 are the records regime. Section 1841 directs the Archivist, within 60 days of enactment, to commence establishing the "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection," consisting of "record copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence (or equivalent subjects by any other name with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects)." Those three terms appear in enacted United States statute with no definitions attached, because the definitions lived in the Senate bill and were dropped. Congress legislated about non-human intelligence and then declined to say what it meant.

Section 1842 sets the mechanics. Each head of a government office had 300 days to review, identify and organize its UAP records; NARA fixed the operative date at 20 October 2024. No UAP record may be destroyed, altered or mutilated, and no record already publicly disclosed may be withheld, redacted, postponed or reclassified. Agencies must give precedence to records "that most unambiguously and definitively pertain to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence," to records under active FOIA litigation, and to records "with earliest provenance." Subsection (g)(2)(D) is the 25-year rule: each record must be disclosed in full not later than 25 years after creation unless the President certifies continued postponement is necessary because of "an identifiable harm to the military defense, intelligence operations, law enforcement, or conduct of foreign relations" of "such gravity that it outweighs the public interest in disclosure."

Section 1843 is where the Senate's design was inverted. Postponement is decided not by an independent board but by "the original classification authority," on "clear and convincing evidence" of one of four enumerated harms.

The JES at page 1330 states the outcome without euphemism: "The agreement does not include the provisions that would establish an independent Review Board, a Review Board staff, eminent domain authority, or a controlled disclosure process."

On 13 December 2023 Schumer told the Senate: "It is really an outrage that the House didn't work with us on adopting our proposal for a review board... Now it means that declassification of UAP records will be largely up to the same entities that blocked and obfuscated their disclosure for decades." He added that multiple credible sources had notified them that UAP information was being withheld from Congress, "which, if true, is a violation of the laws requiring full notification to the legislative branch." Nine days later the President signed the bill and issued a signing statement listing section 1687 among provisions requiring submission of "highly sensitive classified information" to Congress.

claims.text: Section 1687(a) of P.L. 118-31 provides: "None of the funds authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act may be obligated or expended in support of any activities involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations unless the Secretary of Defense has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024."
claims.source: Pub. L. 118-31, sec. 1687(a) (Dec. 22, 2023), text at H. Rept. 118-301 pp. 489-490, https://douglasjohnson.ghost.io/content/files/2023/12/UAP-pages-only--final--from-NDAA--HR-2670--and-Joint-Explanatory-Statement-12-6-23.pdf

claims.text: Section 1687(b) provides that, consistent with DoD Instruction 3204.01 (August 20, 2014, incorporating change 2 dated July 9, 2020), "independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership."

Section 1687(c) defines "appropriate congressional committees" as the congressional defense committees plus HPSCI and SSCI, and "congressional leadership" as the majority and minority leaders of the Senate and the Speaker and minority leader of the House.

The Joint Explanatory Statement to H. Rept. 118-301 records that the conferees amended the Senate provision (sec. 1646) to "Remove the direction to provide information to the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office" before enactment.
claims.source: H. Rept. 118-301, Joint Explanatory Statement, pp. 1311-1312

claims.text: The Joint Explanatory Statement lists six categories the section 1687 prohibition "could cover," including "Recruiting, employing, training, equipping, and operations of, and providing security for, Government or contractor personnel with a primary, secondary, or contingency mission of capturing, recovering, and securing unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or pieces and components of such craft"; "Analyzing such craft, or pieces or components thereof, including for the purpose of determining properties, material composition, method of manufacture, origin, characteristics, usage and application, performance, operational modalities, or reverse engineering of such craft or component technology"; "Actions relating to reverse engineering or replicating unidentified anomalous phenomena technology or performance"; and "Any aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, and electric ion thrust."
claims.source: H. Rept. 118-301, Joint Explanatory Statement, pp. 1311-1312

claims.text: Section 1841(a)(1)(C) provides that the Collection "shall consist of record copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence (or equivalent subjects by any other name with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects)."

The enacted subtitle contains no definitions of "technologies of unknown origin," "non-human intelligence," "temporarily non-attributed objects," "record" or "Collection" — the definitions existed in sections 9001-9015 of the Senate amendment and were dropped in conference, leaving the terms undefined in United States statute.
claims.source: Pub. L. 118-31, subtitle C of title XVIII; H. Rept. 118-301 pp. 568-575 (no DEFINITIONS section appears in secs. 1841-1843)

claims.text: Section 1842(c)(1) required each head of a Government office to review, identify and organize each UAP record in its custody within 300 days of enactment; NARA implemented this as a deadline of October 20, 2024, and stated it would accept only digital versions.

Section 1842(g)(2)(D) requires each UAP record to be publicly disclosed in full not later than 25 years after its first creation "unless the President certifies that (i) continued postponement is made necessary by an identifiable harm to the military defense, intelligence operations, law enforcement, or conduct of foreign relations; and (ii) the identifiable harm is of such gravity that it outweighs the public interest in disclosure."

Section 1843(a) vests the postponement determination in "the original classification authority" on a finding of "clear and convincing evidence" of one of four enumerated harms — restoring the decision to the classifying agency rather than the independent board the Senate had proposed; section 1843(b) permits Senior Agency Officials to withdraw records from the Collection determined to be both unrelated to UAP and properly classified on 60 days' advance notice to congressional leadership and the oversight committees, and section 1843(c) requires notice of any postponement within 15 days.

The Joint Explanatory Statement states: "The agreement does not include the provisions that would establish an independent Review Board, a Review Board staff, eminent domain authority, or a controlled disclosure process."
claims.source: H. Rept. 118-301, Joint Explanatory Statement, p. 1330

claims.text: Section 7343 imposes a parallel funding cutoff on Intelligence Authorization funds, substituting the Director of National Intelligence for the Secretary of Defense and adding the Appropriations Committees to the notification list; its subsection (c) contains a dangling reference to "contracts covered by such instruction" with no instruction identified anywhere in that section.

The chairmen of the House and Senate intelligence committees entered an Explanatory Statement in the Congressional Record of December 14, 2023 stating that section 7343 "is also intended to avoid technology and security stovepipes and expand awareness regarding any historical exotic technology antecedents previously provided by the Federal Government for research and development purposes if they are shown to exist."

In a colloquy with Senator Rounds on the Senate floor on December 13, 2023, Senator Schumer said: "It is really an outrage that the House didn't work with us on adopting our proposal for a review board, which, by definition, needs bipartisan consent. Now it means that declassification of UAP records will be largely up to the same entities that blocked and obfuscated their disclosure for decades," and in the same colloquy: "We have also been notified by multiple credible sources that information on UAPs has also been withheld from Congress, which, if true, is a violation of the laws requiring full notification to the legislative branch, especially as it relates to the four congressional leaders, Defense Committees, and the Intelligence Committee."
claims.source: Cong. Rec., Dec. 13, 2023, pp. S5930-S5931; reproduced at https://douglasjohnson.ghost.io/uap-disclosure-act-pentagon-rewrite-nov-2023/

entityDossier.denialPosture: The Presidential signing statement of December 22, 2023 is the operative denial artifact: it identified section 1687 as one of several provisions compelling delivery of highly sensitive classified information to Congress and reserved to the Executive a construction of those provisions consistent with its own view of national security — a reservation aimed squarely at the one UAP provision with a funding sanction attached.
connections: P.L. 118-31 secs. 1841-1843 are the surviving remnant of S.Amdt. 797, the Schumer-Rounds UAP Disclosure Act; the deletions are itemized in the Joint Explanatory Statement at p. 1330.

Section 1687 aims directly at the waived and unacknowledged SAP mechanism of 10 U.S.C. 119 and DoDI 5205.11 by conditioning appropriations on disclosure to the defense and intelligence committees and the four leaders.
Section 1687(b) and section 7343(c) target contractor independent research and development indirect expense under DoDI 3204.01 — the funding path that bypasses DoD program elements entirely.
The 300-day review obligation runs against every 'Government office,' expressly including the NRO, CIA, DOE and the military departments; NARA set the compliance date at October 20, 2024.

AARO is written into the statute at sec. 1842(c)(2)(E)-(F) and sec. 1842(c)(3) as a recipient of agency records, after conferees removed the Senate requirement that SAPs provide UAP material to AARO under sec. 1687.
Sean Kirkpatrick and OUSD(I&S) are the named actors whose November 2023 redline shaped the conference outcome.
Sec. 7341 shifted the annual UAP report obligation from the Secretary of Defense and the DNI to AARO and its director.

entityDossier.whatItIs: EG&G — Edgerton, Germeshausen and Grier — was founded in 1947 by three MIT-connected figures whose wartime work instrumented and photographed nuclear detonations, and became the Atomic Energy Commission's principal test-instrumentation contractor at the Nevada Test Site. Its Las Vegas-based Special Projects division provided engineering, technical, radar and logistical support to classified programs at the Air Force operating location near Groom Lake and operated the unmarked passenger airline known as Janet from a dedicated terminal at McCarran International Airport. The name and the contracts have since passed through the Carlyle Group, URS Corporation, AECOM and Amentum.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: EG&G is the connective tissue of the American black-site system: the same firm that instrumented nuclear tests ran the workforce airlift, the technical support and the site services that make an unacknowledged installation function. Its employees are the population at the center of the only litigation that has ever forced a court to decide what legal protection a denied facility enjoys. When Groom Lake workers sued in August 1994 alleging illegal open-air burning of hazardous waste, the Secretary of the Air Force filed a formal military and state secrets privilege claim covering categories that expressly included "security sensitive environmental data"; the President signed an annual RCRA exemption for "the United States Air Force's operating location near Groom Lake, Nevada"; and the Ninth Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that seemingly innocuous information forming part of a classified mosaic may be withheld and that a court cannot order the government to disentangle it. That sequence — contractor workforce, denied facility, state secrets, presidential exemption, dismissal — is the complete legal template a legacy program would require, and it is fully documented in the Federal Register and the Federal Reporter.
entityDossier.narrative:
Harold "Doc" Edgerton, Kenneth Germeshausen and Herbert Grier came out of MIT and out of the Manhattan Project's photographic and timing instrumentation work, and in 1947 incorporated the company that carried their initials. EG&G's core business for decades was the measurement of nuclear detonations for the Atomic Energy Commission — high-speed photography, timing and firing, diagnostics — making it one of very few private firms holding continuous clearances into the most sensitive American technical programs. From that base it grew into site services, security support, range operations and personnel logistics across the Nevada complex.

The most visible artifact is the airline. EG&G Special Projects operated the passenger service, universally known by its Janet callsigns, that moves the workforce from Las Vegas to the Air Force operating location at Groom Lake and to the Tonopah Test Range. A Nevada Department of Transportation diagram for McCarran dated May 1999 labels the building on the west side of the field the "EG&G Airlift Terminal." Reporting places the first Las Vegas-to-Groom flights in 1972 with a Douglas DC-6, and current operations at roughly twenty round trips per weekday carrying one to one and a half thousand workers on unmarked aircraft. This is what a routinized, industrial-scale commute to an unacknowledged facility looks like, and it has looked like that for over fifty years.

The legal history is the part that matters most for this board. In August 1994, Professor Jonathan Turley of the National Law Center at George Washington University filed two suits based on field research by the Project on Government Oversight: Frost v. Perry against the Secretary of Defense and Kasza v. Browner against the EPA Administrator, both in the District of Nevada, both under the citizen-suit provisions of the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act. Helen Frost was the widow of a former worker at the site; Walter Kasza was another. Six plaintiffs were permitted to proceed under pseudonyms because, in the district court's finding, "there is a substantial danger here that the Plaintiffs will be subject to retaliation by the government or possible physical attack and harassment from third parties in Nevada."

The government's response was not to deny the allegations. Once discovery began, the Air Force refused to furnish almost all requested information on privilege grounds, and Secretary of the Air Force Sheila Widnall invoked a formal claim of military and state secrets privilege over categories of national security information associated with the operating location near Groom Lake, "specifically including '[s]ecurity sensitive environmental data.'" The claim was supported by an unclassified declaration and a classified declaration reviewed in camera, and the court also reviewed in camera a classified declaration by Air Force Vice Chief of Staff General Thomas S. Moorman, Jr. The district court found the privilege properly invoked and held that it covered the requested information "even though her need for discovery was compelling." The Air Force then moved for summary judgment on the ground that the privilege barred any evidence tending to confirm or disprove that hazardous waste had ever been generated, stored or disposed of at the location — an essential element of every claim. Summary judgment was granted.

On the EPA side, the district court held that RCRA itself contains no exception for disclosure of classified information, but that the President may exempt a federal facility under 42 U.S.C. 6961(a), and gave the Administrator time to obtain one. On 29 September 1995 the President issued Presidential Determination No. 95-45, published at 60 Federal Register 52823, which reads in operative part: "I find that it is in the paramount interest of the United States to exempt the United States Air Force's operating location near Groom Lake, Nevada (the subject of litigation in Kasza v. Browner (D. Nev. CV-S-94-795-PMP) and Frost v. Perry (D. Nev. CV-S-94-714-PMP)) from any applicable requirement for the disclosure to unauthorized persons of classified information concerning that operating location." It exempted the location from "any Federal, State, interstate or local provision respecting control and abatement of solid waste or hazardous waste disposal that would require the disclosure of classified information concerning that operating location to any unauthorized person," and stated: "This exemption shall be effective for the full one-year statutory period." One year. It must be renewed, and it has been.

The Ninth Circuit decided the consolidated appeals on 8 January 1998. Kasza v. Browner, 133 F.3d 1159, cert. denied, 525 U.S. 967 (1998). The panel held that the state secrets privilege is absolute; that "if seemingly innocuous information is part of a classified mosaic, the state secrets privilege may be invoked to bar its disclosure and the court cannot order the government to disentangle this information from other classified information"; and that RCRA section 6001 does not preempt the privilege — "we discern no Congressional intent to replace the government's evidentiary privilege to withhold sensitive information in litigation by providing an exemption from RCRA's regulation of hazardous waste." The Supreme Court declined review.

What that sequence establishes is not that anything exotic was buried in the Groom Lake trenches. It establishes that a contractor-operated installation the government declines to name can be placed outside an ordinary environmental statute by a one-page presidential memorandum; that a cabinet secretary's declaration can foreclose discovery of the physical facts; that federal courts will accept a mosaic theory under which even innocuous data is protected; and that the workers who get sick have no remedy. Every element a concealed recovery and exploitation effort would need to survive litigation was demonstrated in public between 1994 and 1998.

The corporate lineage matters for tracking who holds the contracts today. EG&G's technical services business was acquired in August 1999 by a Carlyle Group entity and operated as EG&G Technical Services; URS Corporation acquired it in August 2002; URS was absorbed by AECOM in 2014; and the Janet operation is reported to have passed with AECOM's federal business to Amentum. The initials survive on the fuselages of nothing, but the function has never been interrupted.

EG&G, Inc.'s Technical Services Division was acquired on August 20, 1999 by ETS Acquisition Corp., a subsidiary of Carlyle-EG&G Holdings Corporation; URS Corporation acquired all of the capital stock of the resulting company on August 22, 2002.

entityDossier.denialPosture: Neither EG&G nor its successors has ever publicly described the Groom Lake work. The government's posture in the Frost and Kasza litigation was not denial but non-cognizability: it did not deny that hazardous waste had been burned, it asserted that the existence or non-existence of such information is a state secret. Presidential Determination 95-45 preserves that posture explicitly, stating that nothing in it is intended to "imply that in the absence of such a Presidential exemption, the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) or any other provision of law permits or requires disclosure of classified information to unauthorized persons."
connections: Groom Lake / the 'Air Force's operating location near Groom Lake, Nevada' — the phrase the Federal Register uses because the installation has no acknowledged name.
Jonathan Turley and the Project on Government Oversight, who built and litigated the only case that has forced judicial findings about the facility.
Secretary of the Air Force Sheila Widnall and Air Force Vice Chief of Staff Gen. Thomas S. Moorman, Jr., whose declarations closed discovery.
President Clinton, whose September 29, 1995 determination created the annually renewable RCRA carve-out.
The Atomic Energy Commission / DOE Nevada complex, where EG&G's clearances and instrumentation business originated.

The Carlyle Group, URS Corporation, AECOM and Amentum — the ownership chain that now holds the successor contracts, all publicly traded or private-equity entities with no separate public accounting for the classified Nevada work.

Kasza v. Browner is one of the most cited modern state secrets precedents and appears in Department of Justice briefing in later privilege cases, making the Groom Lake litigation the doctrinal ancestor of subsequent dismissals.
